title: Candakumara's patience
hook: a fair prince, a grudge, and a father who believes the wrong man
tomorrow: why would a monk call the people who insult him good?

segments.voice: Yesterday, khanti: the elephant feels the arrow and keeps its footing. Today the arrow comes from home.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT KEEPS ITS FOOTING.` → `TODAY: AN ARROW FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Few things sting like being punished for doing the right thing. In the Jataka, Prince Canda is a fair judge. When the royal priest takes a bribe and hands down a crooked ruling, Canda sets it right in front of everyone. The priest never forgives him. He goes to the king, Canda's own father, with a terrible plan dressed up as religion: sacrifice your sons and much of your household, and you will reach heaven. And the king believes him. This one stays gentle: the sacrifice never happens.
screen: `PUNISHED FOR DOING RIGHT.` → `A PRIEST WITH A GRUDGE.` → `AND THE KING BELIEVES HIM.`

segments.voice: Here is where the story spends its time. Canda doesn't raise an army. He doesn't curse his father. Led out bound, he pleads, again and again, gently. Don't do this, father. Make us your servants. Send us away, and we'll go. Spare the others. He never stops treating the king as his father, even when the king has stopped acting like one. That's patience under wrong, and it's harder than patience in a slow line at the store. It isn't agreeing that the wrong is right. Canda says plainly that the plan is crooked. He just refuses to let the injustice turn him into someone else. The tale doesn't make patience magic. The king wavers, then hardens again. At the last moment, the story says, Canda's wife makes a solemn act of truth, and Sakka, king of the gods, appears and stops it. Some readers see the point there: patience held the door open long enough for help to arrive. The Dhammapada has a line for people like Canda. In Max Müller's words: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins."
screen: `HE PLEADS, AND KEEPS PLEADING.` · `STILL HIS FATHER'S SON.` · `NOT AGREEING. NOT BECOMING THEM.` · `HELP ARRIVES AT THE LAST MOMENT.` · then, large: `PATIENT UNDER WRONG.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small unfairness you're carrying. Say out loud, quietly, exactly what happened, in plain words, with nothing added about the person. Then rest your hands open on your knees for the rest of the sit.
Candakumara's patience: a prince who bears a deep wrong without giving up the truth or his gentleness.
Keep this one: patient under wrong, which means not agreeing with it, and not becoming it either. Rest well.

howItsDone: The Candakumara (Khandahala) Jataka is one of the last ten Jataka tales, tied by tradition to the perfection of patience, and is retold in Theravada sermons and temple art.

fork.reveal: Canda says plainly that the plan is crooked, and keeps pleading gently. patience under wrong isn't silence, and it isn't revenge.

Canda.meaning: a prince in the Jataka who bears injustice patiently

Sakka.meaning: king of the gods in Buddhist stories

act of truth.meaning: a solemn true statement, said in the stories to have power

Jataka.meaning: stories of the Buddha's earlier lives

notes: For parents: the story turns on a planned human sacrifice; the hook says plainly it never happens, and the ending (in the Jataka the crowd turns on the priest) is left out.
The villain is named only as 'the royal priest' (Khandahala, the king's purohita); his caste is not named, so the tale isn't read as a judgment on any group. Keeper should confirm the framing.

Jataka 542 paraphrased: Canda's fair judgment against a bribed ruling, the priest's grudge, the king's dream of heaven, Canda's repeated pleas (servitude, exile), the queen's act of truth, Sakka's intervention. Confirm details.
Dhammapada 222 quoted from Max Müller (SBE X, 1881); confirm exact wording. Chosen for its driver image (Mai's storyline).
